analysis.one_liner: Requires USDA to set pathogen limits, test meat and poultry, and order contaminated food recalled.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or any House floor action before the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Agriculture Department to write science-based rules limiting disease-causing bacteria like E. coli and Salmonella in meat and poultry. It would require plants to test their products and report results, set enforceable pathogen levels, allow the government to order recalls of contaminated meat (not just ask companies to volunteer), track animals back to the farms they came from, and fine violators up to $100,000 per day. It also updated animal quarantine and import laws to keep diseased livestock out of the country. The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and its subcommittees but never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats meat or poultry. The bill would have required regular testing for human pathogens, set enforceable contamination limits (with special attention to infants, the elderly, and people with weakened immune systems), given USDA mandatory recall power over contaminated products, and required labels with safe-handling instructions on products not fully cooked [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Agriculture Secretary to issue regulations, within two years, requiring meat and poultry plants to test for human disease-causing pathogens, report the results, and establish scientifically supportable pathogen levels above which products cannot be sold [S3].

Gives the Secretary mandatory authority to order the halt of distribution and recall of meat or poultry that poses a public health threat, including notice to consumers, after companies have failed to do so voluntarily [S3].

Creates livestock and poultry traceback: animals must be identified so contaminated meat can be traced to the premises it came from, with recordkeeping requirements and civil penalties up to $100,000 per day of violation [S3].

Updates animal quarantine, import, and export laws so the Secretary can seize, quarantine, and dispose of diseased animals and restrict imports that could transmit disease to animals or people [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry slaughterhouses and processors would bear the cost of testing, traceback identification and recordkeeping, safe-handling labeling, potential condemnation of noncompliant product, and civil penalties up to $100,000 per day. Some of those compliance costs would likely be passed to consumers in higher meat prices [S3].

drawbacks.text: Mandatory testing, traceback identification, and recordkeeping would impose real compliance costs on slaughterhouses and processors, and condemned product could be a significant loss for plants that fail to meet the new pathogen limits [S3].
Some of the compliance cost would likely be passed on as higher retail meat prices, hitting household food budgets [S3].
Small meat plants might have found it harder than large ones to absorb testing and recordkeeping systems, raising consolidation concerns that the bill does not address [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit is broad and direct: fewer cases of foodborne illness from bacteria in meat and poultry, with the risk to children, the elderly, and immunocompromised people explicitly weighed when setting limits. The costs fall on the industry in compliance and penalties, with some likely pass-through to grocery prices. On balance the bill was designed as a genuine consumer-safety measure, though it left the burdens on smaller plants and the size of price effects unanswered.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and two of its subcommittees in September 1994, but no markup or vote ever happened, and the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 19, 1994 by Rep. Stenholm with Reps. Waxman, Brown of California, and Farr as original cosponsors, and had 6 Democratic cosponsors total [S1][S3][S4].

It was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture, then to the Subcommittee on Livestock and the Subcommittee on Department Operations and Nutrition, and the committee requested executive comment from USDA [S5].
No further action was taken: the bill never received a subcommittee or full committee vote and never reached the House floor before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processors avoided the testing, traceback, recall, and penalty requirements, and the bill's public-health protections never took effect.

sides.party_line_note: The only record is sponsorship: the sponsor and all 6 cosponsors were Democrats, and there was no committee or floor vote to reveal any partisan split [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Meat and poultry processors and slaughterhouses
industries.note: The bill would have required testing for pathogens, enforceable contamination limits, mandatory recalls, and fines up to $100,000 per day. Its defeat left plants free to continue operating without federally enforceable microbial standards, with the health risk borne by consumers.
Traceback rules would have required animal identification and recordkeeping so contaminated meat could be traced to its source. The bill never advanced, so these requirements never took effect.

industries.industry: Meat importers and foreign livestock suppliers
industries.note: Title II would have tightened import restrictions, quarantine, and inspection of animals and animal products that could carry disease. Tighter import controls protect consumers but also restrict importers' business.
